title: Adaptive immunity, antibodies and vaccines
blurb: Compare B and T cells, match each antibody class to its job, explain primary versus secondary responses, and classify immunity as active or passive, natural or artificial.
question: A newborn is protected against some infections for a few months even though she has never been sick, while her mother stays immune to measles for life after one infection. What type of immunity does each have, and why does one fade while the other lasts?

teach.body: Adaptive (acquired) immunity is the third line of defense. It is specific: each lymphocyte recognizes one antigen. It has memory, so a second exposure brings a faster, stronger response. An antigen is a molecule, usually a protein or polysaccharide, recognized as foreign. An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells that binds one specific antigen. Plain English: antigens are the name tags; antibodies are the matching handcuffs.

teach.caption: Both are made in red bone marrow; only T cells move to the thymus to mature.

children.label: Helper T (CD4)
children.sub: Coordinate; activate B and cytotoxic T

teach.caption: HIV destroys helper T (CD4) cells, so AIDS is marked by a low CD4 count and a crippled response.

teach.h: Presenting the antigen, and when it goes wrong
teach.body: Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) show antigen fragments on MHC proteins to T cells. Helper T cells then release cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Failures: hypersensitivity (allergy; anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated and treated with epinephrine), autoimmune disease (attacking self: type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, multiple sclerosis) and immunodeficiency (HIV/AIDS, SCID).

teach.caption: Activated helper T cells also switch on cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected cells directly.
Memory cells make the difference. That is the basis of vaccines and booster doses.

head: Class
Key facts
rows: Most abundant in blood; main secondary-response antibody; only class to cross the placenta
In secretions: saliva, tears, mucus, breast milk; guards mucous membranes
First made in a primary response; largest (pentamer); anti-A and anti-B
Binds mast cells and basophils; allergies, anaphylaxis, parasitic worms

teach.caption: Active: slow to develop, long-lasting, with memory. Passive: immediate but temporary (weeks to months), with no memory.

teach.h: Scenario: baby Amara and her mother
teach.body: Amara's mother had measles as a child: naturally acquired ACTIVE immunity, with memory cells that last for life. Before birth, the mother's IgG crossed the placenta, and Amara now gets IgA in breast milk: naturally acquired PASSIVE immunity. Amara's borrowed antibodies protect her at once but fade within months, because she made no memory cells. Her measles vaccine will later give her artificially acquired active immunity.

teach.text: Plasma cells (from B cells) make antibodies, not T cells. T cells mature in the THYMUS; B cells in bone marrow. HIV destroys HELPER T cells. IgG crosses the placenta; IgM is first in a primary response. Vaccines give ACTIVE immunity; breast milk gives PASSIVE immunity.

items: B cells: bone marrow, humoral, become plasma cells (antibodies) and memory B cells.
T cells: thymus, cell-mediated; helper (CD4, HIV target), cytotoxic (CD8), regulatory, memory.
Primary response: slow, IgM first. Secondary: fast, strong, IgG, thanks to memory cells.
GAMED: IgG placenta, IgA secretions, IgM first, IgE allergy and worms, IgD B-cell receptor.
Active (infection, vaccine) lasts; passive (maternal antibodies, antivenom) is temporary.

summary: You can now compare B and T lymphocytes, explain antigen presentation and the roles of helper and cytotoxic T cells, and match each antibody class to its job. You can also explain primary versus secondary responses and classify any immunity as natural or artificial, active or passive.

A.why: Activated B cells become plasma cells, which secrete antibodies.

whyNot.0: Helper T cells release cytokines that activate B cells; they do not make antibodies.
whyNot.2: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly.
whyNot.3: Memory B cells wait for re-exposure; they become plasma cells only when reactivated.

A.why: T cells are made in red bone marrow but mature in the thymus, which is why they are called T cells.

whyNot.1: B cells mature in red bone marrow; T cells leave it to mature in the thymus.
whyNot.2: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ that filters blood.
whyNot.3: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes meet antigens.

A.q: Which antibody class is the ONLY one that crosses the placenta?
A.why: IgG crosses the placenta, giving the fetus naturally acquired passive immunity.

whyNot.0: IgA reaches the baby in breast milk, not across the placenta.
whyNot.1: IgE is involved in allergies and defense against parasitic worms.
whyNot.3: IgM is the first antibody of a primary response and is too large to cross the placenta.

B.q: HIV causes AIDS by destroying which cells?
B.why: HIV infects and destroys helper T (CD4) cells, which coordinate the immune response; AIDS is a low CD4 count.

whyNot.0: B cells are not HIV's main target, though antibody responses suffer without helper T cells.
whyNot.2: Cytotoxic T cells are CD8, not the CD4 cells HIV destroys.
whyNot.3: NK cells are innate cells and are not the defining target of HIV.

B.q: A breastfed baby receives IgA antibodies in her mother's milk. What type of immunity is this?
B.why: Ready-made antibodies passed naturally from mother to baby give naturally acquired passive immunity.

whyNot.0: Artificial passive immunity is an injection of antibodies, such as antivenom.
whyNot.1: Natural active immunity comes from having the infection and making your own antibodies.
whyNot.2: Artificial active immunity comes from vaccination.

B.q: Which statement about the secondary immune response is CORRECT?
options: It is slower and weaker than the primary response
It is dominated by IgM rather than IgG antibodies
It is faster and stronger because of memory cells
It occurs the first time an antigen is encountered
B.why: On re-exposure, memory cells produce a faster, stronger, longer-lasting response, mainly IgG.

whyNot.0: The secondary response is faster and stronger than the primary one.
whyNot.1: IgM dominates the primary response; IgG dominates the secondary one.
whyNot.3: The first encounter produces the primary response.

C.q: Ms. Patel receives a tetanus booster years after her first vaccine series. Within days her antibody level rises higher than it did after her first dose. Which statement BEST explains this?
options: Memory cells from earlier doses respond quickly
Passive antibodies from the booster last longer
Plasma cells from the first dose kept up full output
IgM made in the primary response returns quickly
C.why: Her first series created memory cells, which mount a fast, strong secondary response to the booster.

whyNot.1: A booster vaccine gives active immunity; it does not contain ready-made antibodies.
whyNot.2: Antibody levels fall after a primary response; the rapid rise comes from memory cells.
whyNot.3: A secondary response is dominated by IgG, not IgM.

C.q: Which example describes artificially acquired PASSIVE immunity?
options: A measles vaccine given to a toddler
C.why: Antivenom is an injection of ready-made antibodies: artificial (medical) and passive (borrowed).

whyNot.0: A vaccine makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory: artificial active.
whyNot.2: Maternal IgG is passive but natural.
whyNot.3: Recovering from an infection gives natural active immunity.

C.q: Which statement about B and T lymphocytes is CORRECT?
options: T cells provide humoral immunity; B cells, cell-mediated
B cells mature in the thymus; T cells, in bone marrow
B cells provide humoral immunity; T cells, cell-mediated
Cytotoxic T cells secrete antibodies against toxins
C.why: B cells give humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity; T cells give cell-mediated immunity.

whyNot.0: This reverses the two: humoral immunity is B-cell (antibody) based.
whyNot.1: This reverses the sites: B cells mature in bone marrow, T cells in the thymus.
whyNot.3: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly; antibodies come from plasma cells.

reteach.title: Think of a detective agency
reteach.question: A witness shows a sketch to a detective, who calls in a SWAT team and a factory that builds tracking devices, then files the case for next time. Which immune cells play these parts?

blocks.body: The antigen-presenting cell is the witness holding up a sketch (antigen on MHC). The helper T cell is the detective who reads it and calls in help. The cytotoxic T cell is the SWAT team that removes infected cells directly. The B cell opens a factory (plasma cells) that makes tracking devices (antibodies) for that one suspect. Memory cells are the case file. A vaccine is a training drill; borrowed antibodies are another agency's devices: useful now, but no file is kept.

blocks.text: Take out the detective and the whole agency stalls: that is why HIV, which destroys helper T cells, cripples both antibody and cell-mediated responses.

explain.body: B cells mature in bone marrow and give humoral immunity through plasma cells and antibodies. T cells mature in the thymus and give cell-mediated immunity.

test.q: Humoral immunity is carried out mainly by
test.why: Humoral immunity is antibody-mediated: plasma cells (from B cells) secrete antibodies into body fluids.

whyNot.1: Cytotoxic T cells carry out cell-mediated immunity.
whyNot.2: NK cells are part of innate immunity.
whyNot.3: Macrophages are innate phagocytes, though they also present antigen.

explain.body: APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) show antigen on MHC. Helper T (CD4) cells activate B and cytotoxic T cells; cytotoxic T (CD8) cells kill infected cells.

test.q: Which cells display antigen fragments on MHC proteins to activate T cells?
test.why: Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells, along with macrophages and B cells.

whyNot.0: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they are not the antigen-presenting cells that activate T cells.
whyNot.1: Red blood cells carry oxygen and do not present antigen to T cells.
whyNot.2: Mast cells release histamine in inflammation and allergy.

explain.body: GAMED: IgG (most in blood, crosses placenta), IgA (secretions, breast milk), IgM (first made), IgE (allergy, worms), IgD (B-cell receptor).

test.q: Which antibody is found in saliva, tears and breast milk, where it protects mucous membranes?
test.why: IgA is the antibody of secretions, including colostrum and breast milk.

whyNot.0: IgG is the main antibody in blood and the one that crosses the placenta.
whyNot.2: IgM is the first antibody made in a primary response.
whyNot.3: IgE binds mast cells and basophils in allergies.

explain.body: Active: your body makes antibodies and memory (infection or vaccine); slow, long-lasting. Passive: borrowed antibodies (maternal or injected); immediate, temporary.

test.q: Which is an example of naturally acquired ACTIVE immunity?
test.why: Fighting off an infection makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells naturally.

whyNot.0: A vaccine gives artificially acquired active immunity.
whyNot.1: Immune globulin is injected antibodies: artificially acquired passive immunity.
whyNot.2: Maternal IgG is borrowed: naturally acquired passive immunity.
